module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
section_skill: Describe AI as a broad term for systems that do thinking-like tasks
outcome_title: Describe AI in plain language as computer systems that perform tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating, and recognize "AI" as a broad umbrella term
intro: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE (AI) is a broad name for computer systems that do tasks we usually connect with human thinking, such as recognizing speech, sorting photos, predicting what comes next, recommending a song, or writing a paragraph. It is an umbrella term, not one machine: a spam filter, a map app's travel-time estimate and a chatbot can all be called AI, yet they work differently and do different jobs. Calling something "AI" does not tell you how well it works or what it can do. To understand a tool, ask what task it performs, what it takes in, and what it gives back.
prompt: Which description fits this course's meaning of AI?
choices: A. Any computer program at all, including a basic pocket calculator | B. A single website that answers questions in a chat window | C. One specific robot that thinks in exactly the same way as a person | D. A broad name for computer systems that do tasks linked with human thinking
correct_answer: A broad name for computer systems that do tasks linked with human thinking
feedback: AI is an umbrella term for many kinds of systems that do thinking-like tasks.
wrong_choices: A: AI refers to tasks like recognizing, predicting, recommending and generating | B: chatbots are only one kind of AI | C: AI is a broad group, not one robot

module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
section_skill: Look past an "AI" label when a decision matters
outcome_title: Describe AI in plain language as computer systems that perform tasks such as recognizing, predicting, recommending or generating, and recognize "AI" as a broad umbrella term
intro: Because "AI" is a broad label, it is used loosely. Marketers may call a simple fixed rule "AI" to sound modern, and some tools that do use learned patterns never mention AI at all. Two products both described as "AI-powered" can differ greatly in quality, cost and risk. When a claim matters, for example when a school, employer or bank says AI helps make a decision, look past the label: ask what the system does, what information it uses, how it was tested, and who checks its results. A label is a starting point for questions, not an answer.
prompt: A budgeting app calls itself "AI-powered," but it only applies one fixed rule: save 10 percent of each deposit. What is the best conclusion?
choices: A. It is more reliable because it says "AI-powered" | B. The label may be marketing; a fixed rule is doing the work | C. It must be learning from millions of other users' data | D. It cannot work, since it is not "real" AI
correct_answer: The label may be marketing; a fixed rule is doing the work
feedback: Labels are used loosely; look at what the system actually does.
wrong_choices: A: a label is not evidence | C: nothing suggests learning | D: a fixed rule can work fine

module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
section_skill: Tell written rules from learned patterns
outcome_title: Tell software that follows rules a person wrote from a system whose behavior comes from patterns learned from examples
intro: Some software follows RULES that a person wrote: "If the total is over 50 dollars, apply free shipping." Every step was decided in advance, so you can read the rule to see why the program acted. Other systems LEARN PATTERNS from examples. A spam filter shown thousands of emails marked "spam" or "not spam" adjusts itself until it sorts new emails well. No one wrote a rule for every case; its behavior comes from the examples it learned from. Rule-based software is predictable but cannot handle cases its rules miss. Learned systems handle messy, varied input but can make surprising mistakes.
prompt: A checkout page gives free shipping whenever an order is over 50 dollars. How was this behavior most likely produced?
choices: A. It learned from many past orders | B. It copied what a chatbot suggested | C. A person wrote a rule for it | D. It guessed the amount at random
correct_answer: A person wrote a rule for it
feedback: A fixed "if over 50, then free" step is a written rule.
wrong_choices: A: a fixed threshold is a written rule | B: nothing suggests a chatbot is involved | D: the result is consistent, not random

module_title: Foundation 1: What AI is and where it appears
section_skill: Tell a model from the product built around it
outcome_title: Tell an AI model from the app or service built around it, and avoid assuming that all AI systems or all chatbots behave the same way
intro: A MODEL is the trained part of an AI system: the learned patterns that turn input into output. A PRODUCT (an app, website or feature) wraps a model with other parts: a screen to type in, instructions the company adds, safety filters, tools such as web search, saved settings, and usage limits. The same model can sit inside several products that behave differently, and one product can switch models over time. So "this chatbot did X" does not mean every chatbot does X, and a product's feature, like saving files or browsing the web, may come from the product, not from the model itself.

choices: A. The app's screen and buttons you tap | B. The company that sells the subscription | C. The trained part that turns input into output | D. The list of usage limits on an account
correct_answer: The trained part that turns input into output
feedback: The model is the learned core; the product wraps it.
wrong_choices: A: that is part of the product | B: a company is not a model | D: limits are set by the product

outcome_title: Recognize overfitting (doing well on familiar examples but poorly on new ones) and what good generalization looks like
intro: A model GENERALIZES when it does well on new examples, not just the ones it trained on. OVERFITTING is the opposite: the model fits its training examples so closely, including their accidents and noise, that it does worse on new ones. intro: A model can only learn what its data shows it, so DATA QUALITY matters as much as the model itself. intro: A LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL (LLM) is a model trained on enormous amounts of text to do one core job: given some text, predict a likely next piece of text. Repeating that prediction, piece by piece, produces sentences, answers, stories or code. Because it learned from so much writing, an LLM can imitate many styles and often produces useful, relevant text. But predicting likely text is not the same as looking up facts or reasoning like a person. An LLM has no built-in way to check truth, so its output can be plausible and wrong. "Large" refers to the size of the model and its training data.

intro: A LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL (LLM) is a model trained on enormous amounts of text to do one core job: given some text, predict a likely next piece of text. Repeating that prediction, piece by piece, produces sentences, answers, stories or code. Because it learned from so much writing, an LLM can imitate many styles and often produces useful, relevant text. But predicting likely text is not the same as looking up facts or reasoning like a person. An LLM has no built-in way to check truth, so its output can be plausible and wrong. "Large" refers to the size of the model and its training data.

feedback: A plausible number still needs a source.
wrong_choices: A: does not check it | C: repetition is not a check | D: precision is not accuracy

intro: People sometimes describe LLMs with extreme claims: "it is just autocomplete, so it can do nothing useful," or "it knows everything, so it is always right." Both mislead. section_skill: Explain tokens and why counts differ from words
outcome_title: Explain tokens as the pieces of text a language model reads and writes, and why token counts differ from word counts
intro: Language models do not read words the way people do. They read and write TOKENS: chunks of text that may be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a space. A common word like "the" is often one token, while a long or rare word like "unbelievably" may be split into several. For English, one provider's rule of thumb is about 4 characters, or about three quarters of a word, per token, but the exact count depends on the model. Token counts matter because limits on how much text a model can handle, and many usage prices, are measured in tokens, not words.

intro: Language models do not read words the way people do. They read and write TOKENS: chunks of text that may be a whole word, part of a word, a punctuation mark or a space. A common word like "the" is often one token, while a long or rare word like "unbelievably" may be split into several. For English, one provider's rule of thumb is about 4 characters, or about three quarters of a word, per token, but the exact count depends on the model. Token counts matter because limits on how much text a model can handle, and many usage prices, are measured in tokens, not words.

correct_answer: Longer text usually costs more tokens
feedback: More text means more tokens, usually more cost.

section_skill: Explain probabilities and why answers vary
outcome_title: Explain that a language model chooses among likely next tokens, so the same request can produce different answers
intro: At each step, a language model gives every possible next token a PROBABILITY: how likely it is to come next. After "The sky is," the token "blue" might get a high probability and "green" a low one. The model then picks a token, often by SAMPLING, which means choosing at random but weighted by those probabilities. That is why the same request can produce different answers on different tries. Some products let users or developers adjust settings, sometimes called temperature, that make choices more predictable or more varied. Variation is useful for brainstorming but means you should not expect identical answers every time.

correct_answer: A probability of how likely it is to come next
feedback: Each candidate token gets a probability.
wrong_choices: B: not what it assigns | C: it weighs options | D: probability is not truth

section_skill: Respond sensibly when answers vary
outcome_title: Explain that a language model chooses among likely next tokens, so the same request can produce different answers
intro: Variation has practical effects. set_title: Fluent is not the same as true
section_skill: Explain why fluent language is not evidence
outcome_title: Explain why smooth, confident language is not evidence that a statement is correct
intro: Language models are trained to produce text that reads naturally, so their answers are usually FLUENT: smooth, confident and well organized. Fluency is not EVIDENCE. A model can describe a book that does not exist, invent a statistic, or misstate a rule in the same confident tone it uses for correct facts. Signs such as precise numbers, formal language or phrases like "studies show" do not prove anything by themselves. To judge a claim, look for something you can check: a source you can open, a calculation you can redo, or a fact you can confirm elsewhere.

feedback: Fluency comes from training on natural text.

intro: A model can only consider a limited amount of text at once, called its CONTEXT WINDOW, measured in tokens. The context usually includes instructions the product adds, the conversation so far, any files or pasted text, and the reply being written. When a long conversation or document exceeds the window, something has to give: depending on the product, older messages may be dropped or shortened, part of a file may be left out, or the request may be refused. The model cannot use text that is no longer in its context, so it may "forget" early details or miss the end of a long document.

intro: A general description of language models cannot tell you exactly how a particular product will behave. Products add their own layers: SYSTEM INSTRUCTIONS the company writes (for example, "be brief" or "do not give medical diagnoses"), SAFETY FILTERS, TOOLS such as web search, code running or file reading, SETTINGS, and LIMITS on length or usage. To know what a product does, test it on your task and read its documentation.

section_skill: Use examples to show what you want, and notice when they pull too hard
outcome_title: Use a short example to show what is wanted, and notice when an example pulls the output away from the written instructions
intro: Sometimes the fastest way to explain what you want is to SHOW it. Adding one or two short EXAMPLES of the desired output, such as a sample product description or a sample quiz question, helps the tool copy the style, length and structure. Use examples that match what you want, label them clearly ("Example of the style I want:"), and say what should differ ("use new topics, not the example's topic").

section_skill: Recognize a hallucination and why it happens
outcome_title: Recognize a hallucination (confident output that is false or unsupported) and why it happens
intro: A HALLUCINATION is AI output that is false or unsupported but presented as if it were true: a made-up quote, a statistic with no source, a nonexistent book, a wrong date stated confidently. It happens because a language model generates likely-sounding text rather than looking facts up, so when it lacks the right information it can still produce something that fits the pattern of an answer. Hallucinations are more likely with obscure topics, very specific details (exact numbers, names, dates, page numbers) and questions about recent events. They are not lies in the human sense; they are errors.
prompt: What is a hallucination in AI output?
choices: A. A deliberate lie the tool chose to tell | B. An answer that is slow to arrive | C. False or unsupported output stated as true | D. A blurry image shown on a screen
correct_answer: False or unsupported output stated as true
feedback: Confident but false or unsupported output.
wrong_choices: A: errors, not lies | B: speed is unrelated | D: not this meaning

section_skill: Spot information that may be out of date
outcome_title: Spot information that may be out of date and check a current, dated source
intro: Information can be OUTDATED even when it was once true. A model's built-in knowledge stops at its training cutoff, and sources it retrieves may also be old. Facts that change often include prices, laws and rules, schedules and opening hours, who holds an office, software features, and records such as "the tallest building." Clues that an answer may be stale: no date given, words like "currently" or "latest" without a date, or a source more than a year or two old for a fast-changing topic. To check, find a CURRENT, DATED source, ideally the organization that controls the fact.

section_skill: Check practical summaries
outcome_title: Compare a summary with its source to find omissions, distortions and added claims
intro: A summary can go wrong in three ways. OMISSION: it leaves out something important, such as a deadline, a cost or an exception. DISTORTION: it changes the meaning, such as turning "may" into "will," reversing a finding, or giving a minor point the main spotlight. ADDITION: it includes a claim that is not in the source at all. Summaries of long documents deserve extra care.

correct_answer: An applicant might miss a key requirement
wrong_choices: A: not true | B: this job requires one | C: they are required

section_skill: Judge a summary by your needs and its balance
outcome_title: Compare a summary with its source to find omissions, distortions and added claims
intro: Some omissions matter more than others. A summary of a lease that leaves out the pet policy may be fine for one reader and a serious problem for another. Decide what YOU need from the document before judging its summary, and ask for those items explicitly ("include all deadlines, fees and penalties"). Also watch for balance: a summary of a debate that gives one side three paragraphs and the other one sentence can mislead even if every sentence is accurate.
prompt: A lease summary leaves out the pet policy. Maya has a dog. What should she conclude?

correct_answer: For her it is serious; she should check the lease
wrong_choices: A: they matter to her | B: they can | C: not shown

section_skill: Spot contradictions and missing information

section_skill: Avoid redaction mistakes
outcome_title: Remove or replace details a task does not need before sharing
intro: Redaction can fail in subtle ways. Blacking out text in some files only covers it visually while the text remains underneath; screenshots of a redacted area or retyping are safer. Placeholders must be consistent: if [PERSON A] becomes [PERSON B] halfway through, the tool may treat them as two people. Replace identifying details with meaningful placeholders instead of deleting everything.

set_title: Permission to share other people's information
section_skill: Decide whether you may share other people's information
outcome_title: Decide whether you have permission to share customer, classmate, patient or workplace information with a tool
intro: Information about other people is not yours to share freely. A customer's order details, a classmate's essay, a patient's chart or a coworker's performance review was given to you for a specific purpose. Before pasting it into an AI tool, ask: Do I have PERMISSION (from the person, or from my school or employer's rules) to share it with this tool? Many schools and workplaces have written rules about which AI tools may be used with which data, and some types of data, such as health or student records, have legal protections. When in doubt, ask before sharing.
prompt: Before pasting a coworker's performance review into an AI tool, what should you ask?
choices: A. Will the tool write a better review than mine? | B. Do I have permission to share it with this tool? | C. Is the review long enough to paste? | D. Does the coworker use the same tool?
correct_answer: Do I have permission to share it with this tool?
wrong_choices: A: not the first question | C: irrelevant | D: irrelevant

section_skill: Understand what settings and deletion actually do
outcome_title: Find and read what a provider says about storing, reviewing and training on your data, and remember practices differ
intro: Policies can be long and vague, so look for specific answers: "Do you use my conversations to train models?" "Can I turn that off?" "How long do you keep data?" "Can staff read it?" "What happens when I delete it?" If the answers are unclear, assume the less private option. Remember that settings protect only what they promise: turning off training may not stop storage, and deleting a chat may not remove copies kept for safety or legal reasons for a stated period. Minimizing what you share protects you no matter what the policy says.

section_skill: Recognize AI-assisted scams and verify through a trusted channel
outcome_title: Recognize scams that use AI-written messages or cloned voices and verify through a trusted channel
intro: Scammers use AI too. AI can write convincing messages with no spelling mistakes, imitate a company's style, and CLONE A VOICE from a short recording, so a call can sound like a relative or boss asking for urgent money or gift cards. Old warning signs like bad grammar are less reliable now. Better signs: URGENCY ("act now"), SECRECY ("don't tell anyone"), unusual PAYMENT methods (gift cards, wire transfers, cryptocurrency), and requests for codes or passwords. The strongest defense is to VERIFY THROUGH A TRUSTED CHANNEL: hang up and call the person or company using a number you already know.

intro: REINFORCEMENT LEARNING (RL) teaches a system by REWARDS instead of answer keys. set_title: Transformers and attention, in plain terms
section_skill: Explain attention in transformers at a conceptual level
outcome_title: Explain at a conceptual level how attention lets a model weigh other words in the context, without treating it as a human mind
intro: Most modern language models use a design called the TRANSFORMER, introduced in a 2017 research paper. Its key idea is ATTENTION: when the model processes one word (token), it can weigh how relevant each earlier word in the context is (when writing, later words do not exist yet). In "The trophy did not fit in the suitcase because it was too big," attention helps link "it" with "trophy." The model computes these weights with math, many times over, in many layers, which lets it track relationships across long passages. Attention is a mathematical weighting of text, not a mind paying attention the way a person does.
prompt: What is the key idea of the transformer design?
choices: A. Following grammar rules typed in by linguists | B. Attention: weighing how relevant other words are | C. Memorizing every sentence ever written word for word | D. Reading only one word at a time with no context
correct_answer: Attention: weighing how relevant other words are
feedback: Attention links words to relevant context.
wrong_choices: A: it learns from data | C: not the key idea | D: attention uses context

outcome_title: Tell searching (finding existing sources) from generating text, and explain retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) simply
intro: SEARCHING finds existing sources, such as web pages, articles or documents, and shows them to you. GENERATING writes new text from learned patterns. Many tools now combine the two in RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION (RAG): the tool first RETRIEVES relevant passages (from the web, a company's files or your uploads), adds them to the context, and then GENERATES an answer based on them, often with citations. Retrieval can make answers more current and specific, but the answer is still generated, so it can misread or go beyond the retrieved text, and the retrieved sources themselves can be poor.

section_skill: Choose between search, generation and RAG
outcome_title: Tell searching (finding existing sources) from generating text, and explain retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) simply
intro: SEARCHING finds existing sources, such as web pages, articles or documents, and shows them to you. GENERATING writes new text from learned patterns. Many tools now combine the two in RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION (RAG): the tool first RETRIEVES relevant passages (from the web, a company's files or your uploads), adds them to the context, and then GENERATES an answer based on them, often with citations. Retrieval can make answers more current and specific, but the answer is still generated, so it can misread or go beyond the retrieved text, and the retrieved sources themselves can be poor.

feedback: Official text comes from a source.

module_title: Everyday: searching and working with documents
section_skill: Check that a source-grounded answer stays within its sources
outcome_title: Check that a source-grounded answer stays within what its sources say
intro: A SOURCE-GROUNDED answer should stay within what its sources say. Checking means three questions. Does each claim have a source? Does the source actually say that, in that strength? Does the answer leave out important limits or exceptions the source includes? Grounding fails in familiar ways: an answer cites the right document but the wrong page; it draws a conclusion the sources do not support even taken together (a valid inference, such as applying a stated discount to a stated price, is fine if labeled); or it adds background "knowledge" with no source at all. A helpful request: "Answer only from these documents; quote the sentence for each claim; say 'not found' if they do not cover it."
prompt: What should a source-grounded answer do?
choices: A. Use as many sources as possible | B. Ignore its sources when it disagrees | C. Stay within what its sources say | D. Add any background facts the tool believes are probably true, even without a source
correct_answer: Stay within what its sources say
feedback: Grounded means supported by the sources.
wrong_choices: A: quantity is not grounding | B: not grounded | D: that breaks grounding

set_title: A document in a request does not retrain the model

section_skill: Explain that a supplied document does not retrain the model
outcome_title: Explain that supplying a document affects that request's context but does not retrain the underlying model
intro: Uploading a document or pasting text gives a model something to READ during your request; it does NOT RETRAIN the underlying model. The text goes into the context for that conversation, so the model can answer questions about it. Other users do not gain that knowledge through the model (though a shared project may let others see stored files), and a new conversation usually will not have it unless the product saves it or you supply it again. Changing the model itself requires training or fine-tuning, which is a separate process. Whether a provider may later use your uploads to train future models depends on its policy and your settings.

outcome_title: Inspect a generated image for visual errors and unreadable or misspelled text
intro: Generated images often contain FLAWS that are easy to miss at a glance. Look closely at HANDS and FINGERS (extra, missing or bent oddly), EYES and TEETH, OBJECTS that melt into each other, SHADOWS and REFLECTIONS that do not match the light, and PATTERNS that break, such as a fence that changes shape. TEXT inside images is a common problem: letters may be garbled, words misspelled ("Bake Sael"), or numbers changed. section_skill: Keep a series consistent and request targeted edits
outcome_title: Keep characters, colors and details consistent across a series, and request targeted edits
intro: When you need a SERIES of images, such as a character on every page of a story or slides with one look, generators often drift: hair color changes, a shirt gets new stripes, the art style shifts. To keep CONSISTENCY, reuse the same detailed description each time ("Mia: short curly black hair, yellow raincoat, round glasses"), keep the same style words, and use reference-image features if your tool has them. section_skill: Make visuals accessible with alt text, contrast and labels
outcome_title: Make visuals accessible with alt text, readable contrast and clear labels
intro: ACCESSIBLE visuals work for more people, including people who are blind or have low vision, color blindness or reading difficulties. ALT TEXT is a short written description attached to an image so screen readers can read it aloud: it says what matters in the image for its purpose ("Bar chart: sales doubled from March to June"), not "image.jpg." CONTRAST means text stands out clearly from its background, such as dark text on a light background. CLEAR LABELS put words on chart lines and parts instead of relying on color alone. AI can draft alt text, but you check it.

section_skill: Fix weak alt text and color-only signals
outcome_title: Make visuals accessible with alt text, readable contrast and clear labels
intro: Generated alt text can be wrong or miss the point: it might describe a chart as "colorful shapes" without the data, or guess at things that are not there. Alt text should match the image's purpose; a decorative border may need none, while an important chart needs its key finding. Color-only signals, such as "red means late," fail for many viewers, so add words or symbols. Some screen readers can recognize text inside images, but not reliably, so give important text as real text or alt text.

section_skill: Tell transcription from speech generation and check transcripts
outcome_title: Tell speech-to-text (transcription) from text-to-speech (generation) and check transcripts for errors and speaker labels
intro: Two audio tasks run in opposite directions. TRANSCRIPTION, also called SPEECH-TO-TEXT, turns spoken audio into written words, for example meeting notes or captions. SPEECH GENERATION, also called TEXT-TO-SPEECH, turns written words into spoken audio, for example a voice reading an article aloud. Transcripts can contain errors: misheard words ("wreck a nice beach" for "recognize speech"), wrong names, missing words when people talk over each other, and wrong SPEAKER LABELS that say who said what. Before relying on a transcript, check names, numbers and key statements against the recording.
prompt: What does transcription do?
choices: A. Deletes background noise only | B. Turns spoken audio into written words | C. Translates text into music | D. Turns written words into a spoken voice
correct_answer: Turns spoken audio into written words
wrong_choices: A: not the definition | C: no | D: that is speech generation

section_skill: Explain provenance labels and the limits of detection
outcome_title: Explain content credentials and watermarks and why missing labels or detector scores are not proof
intro: PROVENANCE means a record of where content came from and how it was changed. CONTENT CREDENTIALS, based on the C2PA standard (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity), attach signed information to a file, such as which camera or tool made it and what edits were applied. WATERMARKS are hidden or visible marks some generators add to their output. These help, but they have LIMITS. Records can be stripped by screenshots or re-uploading. A TOOL-USING WORKFLOW follows FIXED steps that a person designed, using a model for some steps, for example "when a form arrives, summarize it, then email the summary to the manager." section_skill: Build and use test sets in practice
outcome_title: Build a small test set of real tasks with expected answers before trusting a tool
intro: Before trusting a tool for a recurring task, build a small TEST SET: 10 to 20 REAL examples of the task, each with an EXPECTED ANSWER you worked out or confirmed yourself. Include ordinary cases and a few hard or unusual ones. Run the tool on every example, compare with the expected answers, and count how many it gets right. Write down which ones it got wrong and how. correct_answer: They reflect the task the tool will actually face
wrong_choices: A: not the reason | C: no | D: not the reason

section_skill: Avoid test-set mistakes
outcome_title: Build a small test set of real tasks with expected answers before trusting a tool
intro: Test sets go wrong in quiet ways. If you choose only easy examples, the tool looks better than it is. If your expected answers are wrong, you will blame the tool for your error. prompt: A test set contains only easy examples. What happens?
choices: A. The test cannot run | B. Nothing changes | C. The tool looks worse than it really is, since easy examples confuse most AI tools | D. The tool looks better than it is
correct_answer: The tool looks better than it is
wrong_choices: A: it runs | B: it misleads | C: reversed

section_skill: Explain what a benchmark score shows and its limits
outcome_title: Explain what a benchmark score shows, why it may not match your task, and what contamination means
intro: A BENCHMARK is a standard test used to compare models, such as a set of math problems or reading questions with known answers. A high score shows the model did well on THAT test. It may not predict how well the model does YOUR task, which may use different topics, formats or languages. Benchmarks can also be affected by CONTAMINATION: test questions that leaked into the model's training data, so the model may have seen the answers. Researchers (Deng and others, 2024) found contamination can inflate scores and is hard to detect. Use benchmarks as a rough guide, then test on your own examples.

choices: A. A standard test used to compare models | B. A model's price | C. A company's ranking of its own staff | D. A long bench in a computer lab
correct_answer: A standard test used to compare models
wrong_choices: B: no | C: no | D: not the meaning

section_skill: Explain how data can build in bias
outcome_title: Explain how unrepresentative or historical data can lead a model to repeat unfair patterns
intro: Models learn patterns from their TRAINING DATA, so problems in the data can become problems in the model. intro: Estimates differ because they depend on the model size, hardware, how busy data centres are, and what is counted, such as training versus everyday use. The electricity source does not change how much electricity is used, but it strongly affects the related emissions. Newer hardware can use less energy per task, while growing use can raise the total. Claims like "each question uses a bottle of water" may be based on particular assumptions. Look for the source, date, what was measured and the range of uncertainty.

wrong_choices: A: the electricity used is the same | B: the electricity used is the same | C: not a factor by itself
